Case 1: 45-Year-Old Male with Chest Pain: A 45-year-old male presents to the ED with sudden onset severe chest pain radiating to the back. BP is 160/90 in the right arm and 120/70 in the left arm. ECG shows no acute ST changes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A) Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)
B) Pulmonary Embolism
C) Aortic Dissection
D) Pericarditis

[b]Correct Answer: C) Aortic Dissection[/b]

[b]Why C is correct:[/b]
The patient presents with sudden onset, severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back. The classic red flag here is the significant blood pressure difference between the right arm (160/90) and the left arm (120/70). A difference >20 mmHg is highly suggestive of aortic dissection.

[b]Why A (Acute Coronary Syndrome) is incorrect:[/b]
While ACS is a common cause of chest pain, it typically presents with a crushing, pressure-like pain. A massive BP difference between arms is not a feature of ACS. Furthermore, the ECG shows no acute ST changes, making ACS less likely at this moment.

[b]Why B (Pulmonary Embolism) is incorrect:[/b]
Pulmonary embolism usually presents with sudden dyspnea (shortness of breath), pleuritic chest pain, and tachycardia. It does not typically cause a significant blood pressure differential between the arms.

[b]Why D (Pericarditis) is incorrect:[/b]
Pericarditis pain is typically sharp, pleuritic (worsens with deep breaths), and classically improves when the patient leans forward. It does not cause a blood pressure difference between the arms.

[b]Immediate Action:[/b] In suspected aortic dissection, obtain urgent CT angiography. Start IV beta-blockers to control heart rate and blood pressure before giving vasodilators to reduce aortic shear stress.
